text: The assembly will hear an address by his
excellency
Philip Pierre, Prime Minister, Minister
for Finance, Constituency Development,
People Development, Justice and National
Security of St. Lucia. I request
protocol to escort his excellency and
invite him to address the assembly.
Mr. President,
Mr. Secretary General, excellencies,
distinguished delegates,
34 years after the creation of the of
this United Nations, my country St.
Lucia, though small in geography, but
large in courage, dignity, and
conviction took its seat among the
community of nations, brimming with
hope, optimism, and trust in the promise
and goals of this body.
Today we meet at a moment of profound
international uncertainty.
Conflict is spreading, trust is eroding,
developmental gains are being reversed,
and the rules intended to protect
humanity are too often applied
selectively.
For small island developing states,
these crises are not abstract. They are
lived realities.
Climate change threatens our homes,
livelihoods and very existence. Debt
limits are limits our ability to invest
in people. Digital technologies are
transforming our societies without
safeguards.
They can reproduce old patterns of
domination in a new form. And in our own
Caribbean neighborhood, people of Haiti
continue to endure a humanitarian and
sec security crisis that demands more
than statements of concern.
The theme before us, restoring trust,
managing transformation, a United
Nations that delivers for all must not
remain a slogan.
Trust will be restored only when
promises are matched by action, when
commitments are honored, and when the
United Nations delivers meaningful
results for every nation, and when there
is due regard for multilateral
principles, not only for the most
powerful, but for the weakest of us as
well.
This assembly should not be a place
where the world expresses sympathy
without accepting responsibility.
We need action. We need justice. And we
need a renewed international compact
based not on power but on principle. We
need multilateralism,
not unilateralism.
And in the words of the former UN
Secretary General, the United Nations
was not created in order to bring us to
heaven, but in order to save us from
hell.
For St. Lucia, climate change not a
distant environmental issue. It is a
direct threat to national security,
economic stability, food and water
security, and human survival.
While the world focuses on headline
grabbing events like monster hurricanes,
melting glaciers, and tidal waves,
climate change affecting St. Lucia daily
in small but significant ways such as
the unusual bouts of drought in the
rainy season, unprecedented floods in
the dry season, and stifling of our
beaches and coastlines by sargasm.
Our people contribute little to these
global emissions. Yet these events
constantly set back our people's
developmental
and livelihoods and demand that we find
the resources to reverse the damage. St.
Lucia calls for climate finance that
matches the scale of the crisis,
expanded grants and concessional
funding, fast and simple access, full
support for loss and damage, meaningful
debt relief and financing that reaches
vulnerable
people directly.
finance. Climate finance is not charity.
It's about justice, responsibility, and
survival. We must stop confusing loans
to solidarity. A loan is not justice
when a small vulnerable nation is forced
to borrow to repair damage it did not
cause.
A United Nations that delivers for all
must deliver for those on the front
lines of climate change for accessible
finance, concrete support and measurable
results, not merely through
declarations.

a manner that will restore the trust of
the people of Haiti in the United
Nations. Some member states have failed

The Security Council is urged to renew

While gang violence the main factor to
be resolved in Haiti, the crisis in this
country is multi-dimensional.
The international response must include
long-term social economic assistance
that will help restore an acceptable
quality of life for the people of Haiti.
This is why the Caribbean community has

region and beyond. St. Lucia stands with
the Cuban people in their hope for a
better future supported by the

international community.

transformation and consistent with our

St. Lucia supports Taiwan's full
membership in the United Nations.
St. Lucia believes that a truly
inclusive United Nations must ensure
that it decision-making bodies reflect
the world that they serve. St. Lushia
advocates for comprehensive res reform
of the security council to enhance its
legitimacy and effectiveness in
addressing global challenges thereby
restoring trust and a more inclusive
multilateral system. Mr. President, a
21st century United Nations Security
Council could have been more successful
in its responsibility for international
peace and security had it not been
anchored in the world of 1945.
The prolonged reform process must be
concluded quickly and include expanded
permanent and non-permanent membership
for Africa, the Asia-Pacific and Latin
America and the Caribbean regions.
This reform is essential to restore
trust in the United Nations and ensure
it delivers peace and security for all.
St. Luca pledges his commitment and
dedication to work with like-minded
nations to achieve the stated reforms.

On the 25th of March 2026, the General
Assembly approved one of its most
historic and consequential resolutions
that declared the trafficking of
enslaved Africans and racialized shuttle
enslavement of Africans as the greatest
crime against humanity. This resolution
and the subsequent establishment of the
high level global advisory council on
reparatory justice is a very significant
step in the search for reparations for
the transatlantic slave trade and the
enslavement of Africans in the Americas
and the Caribbean. I want to thank the
president of Ghana for beheading and
championing that this resolution. St.
Jusha congratulates the government of
Jamaica on a successful petition to the
British monarch for him to refer three
questions to the judical committee of
the privy council over the legality of
the enslavement of Africans in Jamaica.
Mr. President, reparations are not about
vengeance. They are about truth,
acknowledgement, repair and
transformation. Reparations are not
about seeking charity or re or
revisiting history for its own sake.
History is not behind us when its
consequences remain embedded in wealth,
power, institutions, and and
opportunity. Reparations are about
addressing the continuing effects of
slavery and colonial exploitation,
restoring dignity, advancing
development, and building more equitable
equitable
relationships with the states and
institutions
that that benefited from these systems.
Mr. President,
technology in in its new form of is the

transforming the world. And while it
offers enormous opportunities
opportunities for mankind, it can also
create a new hierarchy in which a small
number of corporations and powerful
states control the systems on which the
rest of humanity depends. We must ensure
that artificial intelligence does not
widen the gap between the powerful and
the vulnerable. Technology must
strengthen aspirations, not quietly
erode them. St. Lucia therefore calls
for strong global standards on data
protection, privacy and artificial
intelligence, equitable access to
digital infrastructure, cyber security
and affordable connectivity.
FE fair technology transfer, transparent

and meaningful participation for small
states in shaping global digital rules.
The digital future must not be owned by
a few. It must be governed for the
benefit of all. Managing transformation
means ensuring that no nation is left
powerless in the face of technological
change.
Mr. President, my country St. Lucia is a
small, open, and vulnerable state, but
our people refuse to impose limits on
their aspirations.
History has blessed us with unimaginable
natural beauty, ambitious friendly
people and two nobel laurates. However,
an unfair international financial system
threatens the very existence of small
states like St. Lucia. The rules
governing global finance affect our
development and our attempt at economic
diversification diversification is
hindered by unfair and unequally applied
rules.
Oceans of water separate us from the
global powers. But our challenges are
mainly connected to decisions made in
the capitals. Emissions released from
these countries affect our climate.
Weapons and drugs traffked for
international networks instigate
violence and gang warfare in our region.
Lack of access to affordable technology
slows our developments.
Mr. President, St. Lucia refuses to give
up. We are educating our people to
ensure that their skills are relevant.
We are modernizing agriculture to ensure
our food security. We are dealing with
the scarcity of water due to climate
change by exploring new sources of
groundwater supply and encouraging
harvesting of rainwater. We are reducing
youth unemployment for the creation of
of a successful youth economy agency. We
are encouraging the spirit of
entrepreneurship by supporting small and
microenterprises
especially womenowned businesses. We are
promoting healthy lifestyles and
universal health care for the provision
of equitable, accessible and affordable
health care for our citizens.
Mr. President, St. Lucia continues to
insist that governance must be about the
improvement of the lives of the people.
We have maintained fiscal discipline,
reduced unemployment as we continue to
create new opportunities and an enable
environment for his for investment in
tourism and other productive sectors.
St. Lucia believes that a better world
is within our reach if we chose
cooperation over coion and ensure that
justice and fairness prevail for all.
The 81st session of the UN General
Assembly must be remembered for turning

commitments and those commitments into
meaningful change. As Mahatma Gandhi
